design_detail: Narrative review (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 2017; read as the NIH author manuscript) of the neurobiology and genetic epidemiology of substance use disorders across alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, cocaine and opioids: twin and family studies (described in words, without estimates), candidate-gene and genome-wide association studies (Tables 2 to 5 list GWAS hits for alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, and cocaine and opioid phenotypes), gene–environment interplay, epigenetics (methylation, microRNA, histone modification, much of it from animal studies), phenome-wide association studies and treatment prospects. The abstract's Methods say only that the literature was reviewed: no databases, dates, criteria or appraisal. Table 1 lists the DSM-5 criteria.
can_establish: How these authors summarized, as of 2017, the direction of twin and family findings (initiation influenced by genes and by shared and unique environment; regular use and dependence more strongly genetic, with shared environment fading after adolescence; liability partly shared across substances), the weak and poorly replicated record of individual genetic variants, and examples of environments that change the size of genetic influence.
cannot_establish: Any heritability figure for any substance use disorder (none is reported; the only twin variance figure is a range of 11–74% for smoking abstinence), the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search), or that genetic influence works mainly through the dopamine system (the genome-wide studies it reviews did not single out dopamine genes).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Studies chosen by the authors; Tables 2 to 5 list genome-wide association results with each study's design, sample size, ancestry and best markers.
sample.selection_effects: No search or selection criteria. The twin evidence is cited without the populations, birth cohorts, sexes or diagnostic methods of the studies, so the reader cannot tell which countries and eras the statements describe. The GWAS tables cover samples mostly of European ancestry, with some African, Dutch, Japanese, Korean and Han Chinese samples, as labelled in the tables.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: twin-model variance components; genotyped variants (single markers, gene-based tests, polygenic risk scores); methylation and gene expression. Phenotypes range from lifetime use and age at first use to dependence diagnoses and symptom counts (Tables 2 to 5).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed as a source of shared liability (3.2) and as a source of phenotypic heterogeneity that weakens association studies (6, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Varies across cited studies (identical vs fraternal twins; cases vs controls in association studies; some opioid GWAS used people who used opioids without dependence as controls, Table 5 footnotes).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed for the cited studies.

outcomes.instruments: Cited outcomes: substance initiation, regular use, dependence (DSM criteria, symptom counts), cigarettes per day, age at first use, alcohol consumption trajectories, smoking abstinence; gene expression and methylation measures.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors name phenotypic heterogeneity (different measures reflecting different stages of use disorder) as a cause of non-replication (6, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Genetic influence: variance attributed to additive genetic effects in twin models, or associations of variants with a phenotype; environment: shared and unique environmental variance in twin models, or measured exposures in gene–environment studies.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no synthesis); the GWAS tables use the cited studies' thresholds (genome-wide significance, or the best markers up to p≤5×10⁻⁶).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates and no twin heritability estimates. Quantities given: polygenic risk scores explained less than 1% of variance in alcohol dependence (Kapoor et al., 2016; Salvatore et al., 2014) and in age at onset of regular drinking (Vink et al., 2014) (4.1, 3rd paragraph); twin studies attribute 11%–74% of the variance in smoking abstinence to additive genetic influences (8 studies cited; 7, 3rd paragraph); a cannabis GWAS meta-analysis of more than 32,000 participants from 13 sites found no single-marker association with lifetime use but gene-based associations with NCAM1, CADM2, SCOC and KCNT2 (4.2, 2nd paragraph). Tables 2 to 5 give per-marker p-values and, where available, effect sizes; many effect-size cells are blank (printed as a question mark).
analysis.selective_reporting: Selection of studies is the authors'; null and non-replicated findings are acknowledged in section 6 and for OPRM1 (4.4) and cocaine (4.3), but the abstract keeps the dopamine emphasis.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors name low power of single-site association studies as a limitation (6, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Qualitative statements about twin findings without numbers; candidate-gene associations that often failed to replicate; genome-wide studies with few replicated hits outside alcohol-metabolizing genes and nicotinic receptor genes; polygenic scores explaining under 1% of variance; a cocaine GWAS with no genome-wide significant dopamine-pathway genes; a null meta-analysis for the much-studied OPRM1 variant in opioid dependence; epigenetic findings that are largely from animals or did not replicate in genome-wide studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that substantial genetic influences on SUD are "particularly important within the dopaminergic system" and that epigenetic studies indicate drug-specific changes in gene expression; the Conclusions say genes regulating the dopamine system have been found to be important (7, 1st paragraph). The body's own evidence is weaker: the cocaine GWAS found no dopamine-pathway genes (4.3), the OPRM1 meta-analysis was null (4.4), few nicotine associations replicated and results of different designs do not converge (6, 1st paragraph), and genome-wide methylation studies did not replicate candidate-gene methylation results (5.2, 4th paragraph). Animal and human findings are interleaved without labels (for example on D2 receptors, 4.1, 1st paragraph, and ghrelin, 7, 1st paragraph). The word substantial is not given a number anywhere in the review.

timeline.event: Heritability in the genomics era: concepts and misconceptions (Visscher et al., 2008), on what a heritability figure does and does not mean; not yet appraised

National Swedish adoption study of registered drug abuse (Kendler et al., 2012): odds ratios of drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, with no heritability estimate; not cited by this review (an editors' cross-reference); appraised in this batch
Common liability to addiction and the gateway hypothesis (Vanyukov et al., 2012); appraised in this round (card sc_vanyukov_2012)
Meta-analysis of twin and adoption studies of the heritability of alcohol use disorders (Verhulst, Neale & Kendler, 2015; on the Alcohol list, not yet appraised).
Multivariate genome-wide association meta-analysis of over 1 million people for liability shared across substance use disorders (Hatoum et al., 2023; on the General list, not yet appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: The review is a 2017 overview of directions, not a source of numbers. Heritability figures for drug use disorders must be taken from primary twin or adoption studies and their meta-analyses, each with its population and era, and read with Visscher et al. (2008) on what such figures mean. The Swedish adoption study appraised in this batch (Kendler et al., 2012) gives odds ratios of drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, not a heritability figure, and is not cited by this review.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PMC author manuscript has no funding, contributors, acknowledgments or conflict-of-interest section. The publisher's version may carry these statements; it was not read.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Virginia Commonwealth University (epidemiology; psychology), University of New England (Australia), Northwestern University. Some cited work is the authors' own: the only twin neuroimaging example (Prom-Wormley et al., 2015), the gene–environment reviews (Dick & Kendler, 2012), work on drug-induced plasticity (Bowers et al., 2010) and the twin-consortium paper cited for shared environment fading in adulthood (Maes et al., 2017). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review and meta-analysis of twin and adoption estimates for each drug use disorder that reports, for every estimate, the population, birth cohort, sex and diagnostic method, tests the twin model's assumptions and looks for change across eras; and well-powered, multi-ancestry genomic studies with independent replication.

domains.note: The Methods say only that the literature was reviewed; no databases, dates or criteria.

No appraisal of the twin, association or epigenetic studies; twin findings are summarized without estimates or sample descriptions; the GWAS tables contain apparent copying errors (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only twin neuroimaging example is the first author's study, the gene–environment section leans on reviews by a co-author, and the 3.1 statement that shared environment no longer matters for regular use or dependence in adulthood cites first Maes et al. (2017), a twin-consortium paper with Prom-Wormley and Dick among its authors, whose reference entry lacks a title; most of the evidence is from other groups.
The abstract and Conclusions give the dopamine system a primacy that the reviewed genome-wide evidence does not show; animal and human findings are interleaved without labels.

domains.domain: Balance of genetic and environmental explanations, and of replicated and unreplicated findings
domains.note: Replication failures and environmental moderation are acknowledged (5.1; 6), but the limits of twin and adoption designs (shared-environment assumptions, the populations and eras sampled, what a heritability figure means) are not discussed; this side is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review has no search or appraisal, gives no heritability estimates, and its abstract claims a dopamine emphasis that the body's own summary of genome-wide studies does not support. It may be cited for its qualitative account of twin findings (initiation vs progression; shared environment fading after adolescence; shared and substance-specific liability), for the statement that individual variants have small effects and replicate poorly, and as a pointer to gene–environment examples, always as second-hand. It may not be cited for any heritability figure or for the primacy of dopamine genes.

key_findings.finding: The review reports no twin or adoption heritability estimate for any substance use disorder; twin findings are given only in words (section 3), and Table 1 is the DSM-5 list of criteria. The only twin variance figure in the review is that additive genetic influences account for 11%–74% of the variance in smoking abstinence across 8 cited twin studies.
key_findings.locator: 3. Twin and Family Studies, 3.1–3.3; Table 1; 7. Conclusions and Future Directions, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The wide 11–74% range for one smoking outcome illustrates how much twin estimates vary between studies; the populations behind it are not described.

key_findings.finding: As summarized from twin studies: initiation of tobacco, alcohol or cannabis use is influenced by genetic and by shared and unique environmental factors; additive genetic influences are larger for progression (regular use and dependence); shared environment is no longer significant for regular use or dependence in adulthood but remains significant in adolescence; genetic influence on regular use and dependence remains after allowing for genes specific to initiation.
key_findings.locator: 3. Twin and Family Studies › 3.1 Genetic and Environmental Effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: As summarized: twin studies point to genetic and environmental factors shared across substances as well as factors specific to each; for initiation the shared factors are mainly environmental, for use and dependence mainly genetic and unique environmental, and the shared influences appear stable over time.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Genetic and Environmental Influences on SUD Across Multiple Substances, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Polygenic risk scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence in two studies and in age at onset of regular drinking in a third; two studies found associations with dependence rather than initiation for both alcohol and tobacco.
key_findings.locator: 4. Genetic Association Studies › 4.1 Alcohol and Nicotine, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cannabis: four GWAS found no genome-wide significant association with cannabis use disorder; a meta-analysis of more than 32,000 participants from 13 sites found no single-marker association with lifetime cannabis use but gene-based associations with NCAM1, CADM2, SCOC and KCNT2.
key_findings.note: Table 4 also lists Sherva et al. (2016) with genome-wide significant markers for a cannabis dependence symptom count, which the text does not mention (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cocaine: although candidate-gene studies focused on dopamine-pathway genes, a GWAS of cocaine dependence found no genome-wide significant association for dopamine-pathway genes. Opioids: the frequently reported OPRM1 A118G association with opioid dependence was not confirmed by a meta-analysis.

The authors list why genetic associations replicate poorly: small effects of each variant, low power of single-site studies, different measures of use disorder, genetic heterogeneity, discovery and replication samples of different ancestry, and subtypes of use disorder; few nicotine-dependence associations have replicated and results of different designs do not converge.
key_findings.locator: 6. Limitations of SUD Genetic Epidemiology Studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Environment changes the size of genetic influence, as summarized: genetic influence on late-adolescent alcohol use is higher in urban areas, in communities with more migration and with more older adolescents and young adults; genetic influence on adolescent smoking is greater with low parental monitoring; the risk linked to a CHRNA5 variant was lower with high parental monitoring; a smoking polygenic score mattered more after more traumatic events and less in neighbourhoods with high social cohesion.

Epigenetics, as summarized: candidate-gene methylation studies report weak differences between affected and unaffected groups, with inconsistent direction for OPRM1; genome-wide methylation studies generally do not replicate the candidate-gene results, alcohol results have not replicated, and none existed for cannabis or opioids; much of the microRNA and histone evidence comes from rats, cell cultures and post-mortem studies.
The authors note that policy changes and changing social norms reduced smoking initiation in the United States, and that how genetic variants bear on such population changes is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the sample size of one study rises by one in each successive row: David et al. (2012) is listed as 32,389, 32,390, 32,391, 32,392, 32,393 and 32,394; the Tobacco and Genetics Consortium (2010) as up to 74,035, 74,036 and 74,037; and one sex-specific row gives 2,060 men, the next 2,062.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): Table 3, rows for David S.P. (2012), the Tobacco and Genetics Consortium (2010) and the BBX and TRPC5 rows
reporting_issues.consequence: An apparent spreadsheet copying error; the sample sizes in the GWAS tables should be checked against the primary studies before use.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives N=12,309 for the study linking KCNC1 and KCNG2 to an opioid dependence symptom count, while Table 5 lists these markers from Gelernter et al. (2014) with N=5,390 and African ancestry; the text does not say that the association comes from that subsample.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): 4.4 Opioids, 2nd paragraph; Table 5
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the text would take the finding to rest on 12,309 people of unstated ancestry; its sample and generality are narrower than the text suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says four GWAS were unable to detect genome-wide significant associations with cannabis use disorder, but Table 4 lists Sherva et al. (2016), a meta-analysis of a cannabis dependence symptom count, with markers at p=4.32×10⁻¹⁰, 1.33×10⁻⁹ and 2.13×10⁻⁸ in an African-ancestry sample of 6,000 (marked not replicated); the text does not mention this study.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): 4.2 Cannabinoids, 2nd paragraph; Table 4, Sherva rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The text and table disagree on whether any genome-wide significant cannabis-dependence finding existed; the table's hits are unreplicated and from one ancestry group.

reporting_issues.issue: Many effect-size and effect-allele cells in Tables 4 and 5 are printed as a question mark, and Table 2 has a malformed marker identifier (ra62338789).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables cannot be used to compare effect sizes across studies.
